**Source:** Sunnybrook Research Institute news release, Toronto, ON, May 9, 2025

**Headline:** "World first: Canadian innovation enhances drug access to brain areas affected by ALS"

## Achievement
- Sunnybrook scientists in the Hurvitz Brain Sciences Program non-invasively opened the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to deliver a small dose of immunotherapy directly to the brain of a patient with ALS. The release calls this a world first.

## Researchers and Roles
- **Dr. Agessandro Abrahao:** co-lead investigator; neurologist, Hurvitz Brain Sciences Program, Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre
- **Dr. Lorne Zinman:** co-lead investigator; director of the ALS Clinic at Sunnybrook
- **Dr. Nir Lipsman:** directed the research; Sunnybrook's director of the Harquail Centre for Neuromodulation and chief of the Hurvitz Brain Sciences Program; described as a neurosurgeon in a photo caption
- **Dr. Kullervo Hynynen:** senior scientist and vice president of research and innovation, Sunnybrook Research Institute; professor, Department of Medical Biophysics, Temerty Faculty of Medicine, University of Toronto
- **Dallan McMahon:** Research Associate
- **Ryan Jones:** Senior Research Engineer-Physicist
- **Other named clinicians and researchers (photo caption, no roles given):** Dr. Pedro Castro, Dr. Isabelle Aubert, Jahan Mookshah, Caroline Giuricich
- **Research team (described):** neurosurgeons, physicists from the focused ultrasound lab, ALS clinician-researchers, imaging research technicians, and an anesthesiologist

## Procedure
- The first of six ALS patients received an infusion of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), then an MRI-guided focused ultrasound procedure to open the BBB over the motor cortex on both sides of the brain.
- The team used the in-house Next Generation Dome Helmet, guided by MR imaging. Sound waves temporarily breached the BBB so the IVIg could enter the brain.

## Drug
- **IVIg:** described as a potential modulator of ALS-related neuroinflammation. The release notes it is not a new drug and has been tested for other conditions, including ALS.

## Trial Details
- **Participants:** six in the first phase
- **Phase:** phase one
- **Primary goal:** test the safety and feasibility of opening the BBB for enhanced IVIg delivery using the Next Generation Dome Helmet
- **Secondary goal:** monitor changes in ALS biomarkers in the brain after enhanced delivery
- **Trial name, registration number:** not stated

## Results and Safety Findings
- Not reported in the content.

## Journal or Publication
- Not stated.

## Next Steps
- The MRI-guided use of the Dome Helmet is an intermediary step toward an MRI-free focused ultrasound device.
- Eliminating MRI guidance would improve patient experience and reduce access and cost hurdles.
- As testing progresses, the helmet will be customizable to each patient's head shape, so patients would no longer need to shave their hair or have the helmet screwed in.

## Quotes
- **Abrahao:** "For the first time in ALS, we were able to temporarily disrupt this barrier in order to allow the drug flow through."
- **Zinman:** "This innovation could be a game-changer for ALS"
- **Hynynen:** "This new helmet provides enhanced image guidance, faster treatment times and targeting capacity"
- **Neal F. Kassell, MD (Founder and Chairman, Focused Ultrasound Foundation):** "This world-first clinical trial highlights both the promise of focused ultrasound"

## Funding
- **Research:** Focused Ultrasound Foundation, ALS Society of Canada, Brain Canada, ALS Association. Also cited: Canadian Institutes of Health Research and National Institutes of Health.
- **Equipment:** Weston Family Foundation, WB Family Foundation, Gerald & Carla Connor, Temerty Foundation

## Background
- **ALS:** also known as Lou Gehrig's disease; a neurodegenerative disorder affecting nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. There is no cure, and average life expectancy is two to five years after diagnosis.
- **Sunnybrook:** home to the largest ALS treatment centre in Canada. In 2016, it became the first Canadian Centre of Excellence in Focused Ultrasound. In 2019, researchers used MRI-guided focused ultrasound to open the BBB in four ALS patients.

## Media Contacts
- Nadia Norcia, Communications Advisor, Research, 416.480.4040
- Anna McClellan, Communications Advisor, Public Affairs

Every tab in the workspace now uses one shared header, `PageHeader` in `frontend/src/components/page-header.tsx`. It's the card panel with a breadcrumb line, the title in one size, an optional description, and space for buttons on the right. The type check shows no new errors; the only ones left are the ones already in `overview-dashboard.tsx`. I haven't looked at the tabs in a browser.

**Before**, the headers came in four styles:

| Tabs | Header |
|---|---|
| The five pipeline steps | card panel, title `2–3rem` |
| Runs & reports and Focused ultrasound | card panel, title `2.25–3.25rem` |
| Patient monitoring | card panel, title `2.5–3.75rem` |
| The 10 "coming soon" tabs | no card, title up to `4.5rem`, extra top padding |

**Now** they all match:
- **Title size:** one size everywhere, the one the pipeline steps already used, since they're most of the tabs.
- **Spacing:** the same 12px gap below the header on every tab.
- **Pipeline steps:** the shared header keeps their run badge and the "Finish this step" / "Clear run" buttons.
- **Coming soon tabs:** they now use the same full-width container as the finished tabs. The "Coming soon" card is smaller to fit.
- **Patient monitoring breadcrumb:** I changed it from "Patient / Motor-function monitoring" to "Library / Patient monitoring", so it follows the sidebar's group and label like every other tab. The patient's name, description and medication line are unchanged.

The only other places using the large brand font are the "addo labs" logo in the sidebar and on the landing page, which I left alone.
